extracted.intended_audience: policy researchers, empirical legal scholars, patent scholars, and USPTO/patent office analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Difference-in-differences empirical study measuring how the Supreme Court's Alice decision and subsequent USPTO guidance (Berkheimer memo, 2019 PEG) affected (1) the probability of receiving a first-office-action Section 101 rejection and (2) first-action examination uncertainty across technologies. Uses USPC grouping to define treatment (Alice-affected) and control groups and performs robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability of a first office action Section 101 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The likelihood/probability that a patent application receives a first office action containing a rejection for patent-ineligible subject matter under Section 101. Estimated as the main dependent variable using difference-in-differences (interaction Alice x PatGrp). Example estimate: Alice increased this probability by 4.66 percentage points (0.0466) for Alice-affected technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret coefficients on treatment interactions as percentage-point changes in probability. Report robust standard errors and statistical significance (*** p<0.01, ** p<0.05, * p<0.1). To express as percent change relative to baseline use the DID percent-change formula ((t2−t1)−(c2−c1))/c1*100. Control for time and technology fixed effects and relevant application/examiner covariates.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-action examination uncertainty (variance across examiners)
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure of variation/uncertainty in Section 101 determinations across examiners at the first-office-action stage (reported as variance or standard deviation). The paper reports percent increases in this metric attributable to events (e.g., Alice increased variance by roughly 61% using the pre-Alice standard deviation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate using cross-examiner variance aggregated at appropriate time-technology units. Include controls such as number of applications, number of examiners, avg applications per examiner, and within-examiner variance. When reporting percent increases, divide the estimated change by a reference standard deviation (e.g., pre-event std dev) and multiply by 100. Check robustness to dataset restrictions because shrinking sample sizes can mechanically inflate variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application abstractness measure
rubrics_metrics.description: A language-based measure of how abstract an application's text is (used at application- or technology-aggregation level). Higher abstractness is associated with higher probability of Section 101 rejection: a one standard deviation increase in abstractness leads to a ~0.58 percentage-point increase in §101 rejection probability (coefficient reported 0.528).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include abstractness as a covariate and interact it with treatment/event indicators to assess heterogeneous effects. When interpreting interaction effects, multiply the estimated coefficient by the relevant standard deviation to obtain percentage-point impact. Be cautious: including higher-order interactions with abstractness may induce multicollinearity and inflate standard errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple-interaction for heterogeneous treatment (Alice x PatGrp x Abstractness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that interacts the treatment indicator, the Alice-affected technology group, and the application/aggregate abstractness measure to estimate whether the Alice effect is larger for more abstract applications (reported coefficient 1.364 in the paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use triple interaction coefficients to compute total marginal effects by adding main and interaction terms evaluated at the mean or one standard deviation of abstractness (e.g., total = β1 + β3 * mean_abstractness). Watch for multicollinearity: triple interactions can dramatically increase standard errors and make some coefficients statistically insignificant even if the main effect remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-trends assumption for difference-in-differences
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that, prior to the event (Alice), the time-by-treatment interaction terms are not statistically different from zero—i.e., treatment and control groups follow parallel trends before the event. The paper states the pre-trend assumption is satisfied (no statistically different pre-Alice coefficients using 95% CI for most months/half-years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test pre-trends by plotting coefficients for leads (month/half-year interactions) and conducting joint F-tests on pre-event interaction terms. Choose an appropriate base period (e.g., May 2014 or first half of 2014). If pre-trends fail, reconsider causal interpretation or adjust specification (e.g., allow differing linear trends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness via dataset restrictions (filed-before-events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restricting the sample to patent applications filed before the events of interest to limit post-event filing behavior and the influence of other decision makers. The paper restricts to applications filed before the events to analyze first-action outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of left censoring: restricting by filing series numbers (e.g., series starting with 12–15) causes the fraction of first-action rejections observed in the dataset to decrease over time. Add covariates (number of applications, number per examiner) and flexible time indicators to mitigate mechanical effects on variance and selection. Re-estimate using different time windows (e.g., 2013–2015) as sensitivity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of other rejection types (§102, §103, §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the event (Alice) affected other rejection grounds (novelty §102, non-obviousness §103, and §112 clarity/enablement). The expectation is that Alice should not affect these because it clarified subject-matter eligibility, not novelty or obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate analogous DID specifications for §102/§103/§112 rejection rates and their examination uncertainty. Look for discontinuous jumps or persistent changes post-event; absence of statistically significant jumps supports the claim that Alice specifically affected §101 and not other grounds. Rely on USPTO compact prosecution policy (examiners issue all grounds in first action) when interpreting substitution arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-event effect checks (Berkheimer memo and 2019 PEG)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the impact of intermediate policy signals (Berkheimer memorandum, 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance) on §101 rejection rates and examination uncertainty using DID-style interactions (e.g., Berkheimer x PatGrp, 2019 PEG x PatGrp). The paper finds Berkheimer reduced §101 rejections modestly (-0.0157) and 2019 PEG had a larger reduction (-0.116).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include separate event indicators for non-supreme-court policy changes. Interpret negative coefficients as reductions in rejection probability/uncertainty. Compute percent reductions over a chosen window (e.g., 12 months) using the DID percent-change formula. Do not include application-level covariates for some event-window estimates if earlier justification states so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression specification and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard regression elements recommended/used: include time fixed effects (Month x Year or Half Year), technology fixed effects (USPC), and possibly examiner fixed effects; include covariates such as avg number of independent claims, avg word count in claims, avg examiner variance, number of examiners, number of applications, avg applications per examiner, and variance in abstractness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report observations, R-squared, and use robust standard errors. Choose fixed effects that capture seasonality and technology heterogeneity (month-year and USPC are used here). When adding many covariates, monitor changes in magnitude and significance of main treatment terms to assess robustness and potential multicollinearity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical-significance notation and robust standard errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use robust standard errors (reported in parentheses) and a consistent significance notation: *** p<0.01, ** p<0.05, * p<0.1. Example: coefficient 0.0466*** (0.00148).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always present standard errors alongside point estimates. Use these conventional significance stars and explicitly state that standard errors are robust. When interpreting small p-values with large samples, also consider effect sizes (percentage-point changes) for substantive importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of DID percent-change
rubrics_metrics.description: Formula described to convert DID absolute changes into percent changes relative to the baseline control group's rate: percent_change = ((t2−t1) − (c2−c1)) / c1 * 100, where t1/t2 are treatment-group averages at pre/post dates and c1/c2 are control-group averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this formula to report percent increases/decreases (e.g., 31% increase in §101 rejection probability through Dec 2015). Clearly state the reference period and group used for c1 to avoid ambiguity. This is a DID-derived relative percent calculation, not a simple relative change of a single group's rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of coefficient plots across time indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot point estimates for treatment × time period interactions across months or half-years to visualize timing, persistence, and pre-trend behavior (figures show monthly or half-year coefficients with a base period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a clear base period (e.g., May 2014 or 2014h1). Use confidence intervals to assess whether pre-event coefficients are statistically different from zero. Such plots help demonstrate a sharp change immediately after the event and test the parallel-trends assumption visually and statistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset construction and left-censoring caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Office Action Research Dataset for Patents used here includes applications with series numbers starting with 12–15 (not all applications in a fixed calendar period), causing left censoring and a mechanical decline over time in the percentage of first-action rejections observed in the dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using this dataset, document the series-number-based inclusion rule and its implications (declining coverage of first actions over time). Account for this in robustness checks, include covariates capturing the shrinking pool (number of applications, avg applications per examiner), and interpret temporal variance measures cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment/control definition via USPC grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'Alice-affected' and 'other technologies' groups by mapping three-digit U.S. Patent Classification (USPC) numbers to treatment or control. The paper provides an extensive table listing which USPCs are Alice-affected vs other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a transparent and replicable mapping from USPC to treatment/control. Report the included classes and justify grouping decisions. Sensitivity checks could reassign or drop borderline classes to test robustness of results to the grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution policy assumption for interpreting substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO compact prosecution policy trains examiners to issue all grounds of rejection on the first office action, implying that examiners should not 'substitute away' from other rejections when issuing more §101 rejections after Alice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this policy assumption when interpreting whether higher §101 use implies reduced use of §102/§103/§112. Still empirically test other-ground rejection rates; absence of change in these rates supports the non-substitution interpretation. Cite USPTO MPEP section (e.g., s2103) when relying on this policy argument.
